thread.title: Top 1 percent rake in 82% of economic, stock gains — the poor tread water

author: Mike Sunnucks
title: Top 1 percent rake in 82% of economic, stock gains — the poor tread water
text: – Senior Reporter, Phoenix Business Journal Jan 22, 2018, 10:17am MST The richest 1 percent took in 82 percent of the wealth gained last year while the poorest 3.7 billion people in the world didn’t gain a penny. That is a according to a new wealth report by Oxfam, a British-based charity focused on poverty. The control of wealth creation by the top 1 percent comes as stock markets continue to hit record under President Donald Trump . The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq have set numerous record highs since Trump took office. The Dow passed 26,000 for the first time earlier this month. U.S. stock markets have gained $6.9 trillion since Trump took office last year, according to CNBC and Bespoke Investment Group. But most of those gains are going to the wealthy, according to various studies including from Credit Suisse (NYSE: CS) New York University economist Ed Wolff estimates 80 percent of stocks are owned by the top 10 percent, according to the Washington Post. Amazon.com (Nasdaq: AMZN) founder and CEO Jeff Bezos has seen his wealth jump to $110 billion with the company’s stock price approaches $1,300 per share. In Arizona, private sector wages did improve 6.2 percent in 2017, according to the Arizona Office of Economic Opportunity. That’s better than the pedestrian 2.6 percent wage growth seen nationally. The statewide gains were propelled somewhat by voters approving a minimum wage increase in 2016. That took Arizona wages from $8.05 per hour to $10 per hour last year and $10.50 per hour this year. The average wage for an Arizona worker in finance, for example, was $29.01 per hour last year. That translated to just over $60,340 annually and was up 4.4 percent over 2016, according to state economists. Workers at restaurants, hotels and bars averaged a $14.97 wage. That was up 5.3 percent from 2016 and works out to $31,138 for a full-time job. A number of employers — including some big Arizona ones such as American Airlines (Nasdaq: AAL), Bank of America (NYSE: BAC), Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (NYSE: WMT) and Western Alliance Bancorp. (NYSE: WAL) — have given employees bonuses or raised pay after Trump and Congress passed tax cuts slicing corporate rates from 35 percent down to 21 percent. Apple Inc. (Nasdaq: AAPL) is giving its employees $2,500 in stock as it repatriates $250 billion from offshore tax shelters and pays a one-time 15 percent rate under the Trump tax cuts. Apple plans on investing $350 billion in the U.S. economy. But still, there are many U.S. workers employed part-time and haven’t seen significant raises. In Arizona, close to 40 percent of working age adults aren’t in jobs or looking for work. Oxfam worries the current stock and economic boom — which could see 4 percent GDP growth in the U.S. this year — isn’t helping those at the economic bottom. “There’s a billionaire boom but most people are treading water in a stagnant global economy,” said Paul O’Brien, Oxfam America’s Vice President for Policy and Campaigns. “A perfect storm is driving up the bargaining power of those at the top while driving down the bargaining power of those at the bottom.” – Senior Reporter, Phoenix Business Journal Jan 22, 2018, 10:17am MST
